# SK2043 — The hash code depends on state that can change

<!-- Generated from Rules/Rikarin.Skala.Rules.Metadata/rules.json. Do not edit. -->

`GetHashCode` on a class reads an equality-relevant instance member that can still be assigned after construction.

| | |
|---|---|
| Category | Correctness |
| Default severity | warning |
| Scope | Semantic |
| Needs a compilation | yes |
| Fix | no |
| Language version floor | — |
| Since | 1.3 |
| Supersedes | S2328 |

## Why

An object whose hash changes after it was stored is lost inside its own dictionary. The bucket was chosen with the old hash and every lookup computes the new one, so the entry is present and unreachable: `Remove` returns `false`, `Count` still counts it, `ContainsKey` says no and enumeration says yes. Nothing throws and nothing logs, and the report that comes back is that an item "disappeared" — which sends the reader to the collection rather than to the key.

## Example

Instead of:

```csharp
sealed class Session {
    public string User { get; set; } = "";

    public override bool Equals(object? other) => other is Session session && session.User == User;

    public override int GetHashCode() => User.GetHashCode();
}
```

Write:

```csharp
sealed class Session {
    public string User { get; init; } = "";

    public override bool Equals(object? other) => other is Session session && session.User == User;

    public override int GetHashCode() => User.GetHashCode();
}
```

## When it does not fire

⚠ **Classes only.** A struct is copied into the collection, so mutating the original cannot move the stored copy; the hazard this rule names needs reference identity to exist at all, and reporting it on structs would be reporting a different, much weaker thing under the same message. ⚠ **A private field that nothing assigns outside a constructor is not reported, even though it is not marked `readonly`.** That is the largest false-positive class in this shape and it is decidable rather than guessed: a private member can only be assigned inside the type's own declaration, so the assignments — including `++`, compound assignment and `ref`/`out` arguments — can be counted. Only a type declared in one file is examined, because that count is only complete for one. `readonly` fields, `const`s, statics, getter-only auto-properties and `init`-only auto-properties are never reported: none of them can change after the object exists. A property whose setter is not private is reported without the assignment scan, because any assembly can call it. ⚠ **The member must also be one the type's equality compares**, and that is what keeps this rule and `SK2042` from arguing over one span: a member the hash reads is either compared by `Equals`, and then mutability is the open question and it is asked here, or it is not compared, and then the finding is `SK2042`'s. The partition is total and neither rule filters the other. A type that declares no `Equals` at all, or whose equality set could not be read, has every hashed member examined here and nothing reported by `SK2042`. Fixless — `readonly` is not an available repair, because the rule only fires where something does assign the member; whether to freeze the state, drop the member from the hash, or stop using the type as a key is a design decision with three different blast radii. ⚠ **A type whose base list did not bind is withdrawn, and that was found by measuring rather than by reading.** On the reference trees a class declaring `IEquatable<Self>` was reported for not implementing it: without the SDK's implicit global usings the name bound to an *error* type, so the interface list held `IEquatable<>` and the comparison against `System.IEquatable`1` failed. Skala loads a compilation three ways and two of them can be incomplete, so an error type among a type's bases or interfaces now withdraws it from every rule in this batch — the same discipline `SK7080` uses for an inheritance chain it cannot walk.
